questions.title: Which of the following is NOT a content of the deep perineal pouch in the male?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a content of the deep perineal pouch in the male?

explanations.A: Correct. The bulb of the penis lies in the superficial perineal pouch, attached to the inferior surface of the perineal membrane and covered by bulbospongiosus; it is not a content of the deep perineal pouch, which lies between the two fascial layers of the urogenital diaphragm above the perineal membrane. This is a common source of confusion because the bulb sits immediately below the deep pouch, on the other side of the perineal membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The membranous urethra pierces the deep perineal pouch as it passes from the prostate to the bulb of the penis, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The paired bulbourethral (Cowper) glands lie within the substance of the deep perineal pouch, embedded in the external urethral sphincter, with ducts that cross the perineal membrane to open into the bulbous urethra.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae) is a genuine skeletal-muscle content of the deep perineal pouch, encircling the membranous urethra.

questions.title: The prostatic urethra emerges from the prostate at its apex through which surface?
questions.question: The prostatic urethra emerges from the prostate at its apex through which surface?

explanations.A: Correct. The urethra enters the prostate at the middle of its base (posteriorly placed) and runs through the gland to leave at the apex through its anteroinferior part, so the urethra emerges anteriorly relative to the apex. This anterior-apex exit point is a useful landmark during radical prostatectomy, where the urethra must be divided cleanly at the apex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior surface of the prostate is related to the rectum and is where the ejaculatory ducts enter, not where the urethra exits.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The base of the prostate is where the urethra enters (from the bladder neck), not where it emerges.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lateral surfaces of the prostate are related to levator ani, not to the urethra course.

questions.title: Which lobe of the prostate lies posterior to the upper (proximal) part of the prostatic urethra, between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts?
questions.question: Which lobe of the prostate lies posterior to the upper (proximal) part of the prostatic urethra, between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts?

explanations.A: Correct. The median (middle) lobe is a wedge of glandular tissue that lies between the urethra anteriorly and the two ejaculatory ducts posteriorly, immediately below the bladder neck; its enlargement in benign prostatic hyperplasia can project into the bladder as a "ball valve" and obstruct the internal urethral orifice. This wedge is the site of the classic bladder-neck "ball-valve" obstruction seen when the median lobe enlarges in benign prostatic hyperplasia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior lobe lies posterior to the urethra as a whole and below the ejaculatory ducts, not sandwiched between the upper urethra and the ducts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The two lateral lobes flank the urethra on either side and form the bulk of the gland; they are not the wedge specifically between urethra and ejaculatory ducts.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior lobe (isthmus) is a small fibromuscular band anterior to the urethra with little or no glandular tissue.

questions.title: The lumbosacral trunk, which descends into the pelvis to join the sacral plexus, is formed by the ventral rami of which spinal nerves?
questions.question: The lumbosacral trunk, which descends into the pelvis to join the sacral plexus, is formed by the ventral rami of which spinal nerves?

explanations.A: Correct. The lumbosacral trunk is formed by the smaller, descending part of the L4 ventral ramus joining the whole L5 ventral ramus; it crosses the pelvic brim anterior to the sacroiliac joint to join S1 and contribute to the sacral plexus, linking the lumbar and sacral plexuses functionally. This partial contribution explains why the lumbosacral trunk is often drawn as the structural bridge linking the two plexuses on diagrams.
explanations.B: Incorrect. L2 and L3 ventral rami contribute to the lumbar plexus proper (e.g., obturator and femoral nerves), not the lumbosacral trunk.
explanations.C: Incorrect. L3 contributes to the lumbar plexus, not the lumbosacral trunk; only part of L4 descends to join L5.
explanations.D: Incorrect. S1 and S2 are sacral plexus roots that the lumbosacral trunk joins, not the rami that form the trunk itself.

questions.title: Which of the following arteries arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery?
questions.question: Which of the following arteries arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery?

explanations.A: Correct. The obturator artery is a visceral/parietal branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery; it runs forward on the lateral pelvic wall to leave the pelvis through the obturator canal. Remembering "anterior division = mostly visceral pelvic branches, posterior division = mostly parietal wall branches" helps sort obturator from its posterior-division counterparts quickly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The iliolumbar artery arises from the posterior division and ascends to supply the iliacus and psoas region.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lateral sacral arteries arise from the posterior division and supply the sacral canal contents and overlying skin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior gluteal artery is the largest branch of the posterior division, leaving the pelvis above piriformis.

questions.title: Which artery anastomoses with the uterine artery to help supply the vagina?
questions.question: Which artery anastomoses with the uterine artery to help supply the vagina?

explanations.A: Correct. The vaginal artery (usually a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac, or of the uterine artery itself) descends on the vagina and anastomoses with the descending cervical branch of the uterine artery, forming a longitudinal anastomotic channel ("azygos artery of the vagina") that supplies the vaginal walls. This anastomotic chain running down the lateral vaginal wall is sometimes called the azygos artery of the vagina.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ovarian artery anastomoses with the ascending (tubal/ovarian) branch of the uterine artery near the ovary and tube, not specifically to supply the vagina.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The obturator artery supplies the obturator region and hip muscles, not the vagina.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior epigastric artery supplies the anterior abdominal wall, unrelated to vaginal supply.

questions.title: Which structure is directly related to the posterior surface of the prostate?
questions.question: Which structure is directly related to the posterior surface of the prostate?

explanations.A: Correct. The posterior surface of the prostate is separated from the rectal ampulla only by the rectovesical (Denonvilliers) fascia, which is why the prostate is palpable and biopsied through the anterior rectal wall on digital rectal examination. This single-fascial-layer separation is also why locally advanced prostate cancer can directly invade the rectal wall.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The urinary bladder is related to the base (superior surface) of the prostate, not its posterior surface.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pubic symphysis lies anterior to the prostate, connected via the puboprostatic ligaments, not posteriorly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Levator ani is related to the inferolateral surfaces of the prostate, not specifically its posterior surface.

questions.title: The space bounded above by the superior fascial layer of the urogenital diaphragm and below by the perineal membrane (inferior fascia) is called the?
questions.question: The space bounded above by the superior fascial layer of the urogenital diaphragm and below by the perineal membrane (inferior fascia) is called the?

explanations.A: Correct. The deep perineal pouch is the closed compartment sandwiched between the superior and inferior fascial layers of the urogenital diaphragm; it houses the membranous urethra, external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscles and the bulbourethral glands in the male. The mnemonic "deep is above the membrane, superficial is below it" keeps the two perineal pouches from being reversed on exam.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superficial perineal pouch lies below the perineal membrane, between it and Colles' fascia, and contains the root structures of the external genitalia (bulb and crura), not the space above the membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ischiorectal fossa is a fat-filled space lateral to the anal canal, unrelated to the urogenital diaphragm's two fascial layers.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The retropubic space lies between the pubic bones and the bladder, well above the perineum.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT a content of the spermatic cord?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a content of the spermatic cord?

options.B: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve

explanations.A: Correct. The ilioinguinal nerve travels through the inguinal canal alongside the spermatic cord, lying on its anterior surface outside its fascial coverings, and emerges through the superficial inguinal ring separately; it is not enclosed within the cord's coverings and so is not classed as one of its contents. Only the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve pierces the deep inguinal ring to travel inside the cord itself, which is the detail that separates it from the ilioinguinal nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve pierces the deep inguinal ring to run within the cord (supplying cremaster and scrotal skin) and is a true content.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The testicular artery, a direct branch of the abdominal aorta, is a core content of the spermatic cord.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pampiniform venous plexus, draining the testis, is a major content of the cord.

questions.title: Which of the following nerves is NOT a branch of the sacral plexus?
questions.question: Which of the following nerves is NOT a branch of the sacral plexus?

explanations.A: Correct. The obturator nerve (L2-L4) is a branch of the lumbar plexus, formed in the substance of psoas major and leaving the pelvis through the obturator canal; it does not arise from the sacral plexus. Remembering the obturator nerve as "L2-L4, lumbar plexus, exits via the obturator canal" separates it cleanly from the sacral plexus branches that exit via the greater sciatic foramen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sciatic nerve (L4-S3) is the largest branch of the sacral plexus, leaving the pelvis below piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) is a sacral plexus branch supplying the perineum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1) is a sacral plexus branch leaving above piriformis to supply the gluteus medius, minimus and tensor fasciae latae.

questions.title: Which artery is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery?
questions.question: Which artery is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery?

explanations.A: Correct. The superior gluteal artery is the largest and most direct continuation of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery, leaving the pelvis above piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen to supply the gluteal muscles. Because it is the only major artery to leave through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis, the superior gluteal artery is a useful landmark for that muscle during posterior hip surgery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The obturator artery arises from the anterior division, supplying the medial thigh via the obturator canal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inferior vesical artery (male) is an anterior-division visceral branch supplying the bladder base, prostate and seminal vesicles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The uterine artery is an anterior-division visceral branch in the female.

questions.title: The seminal vesicles are located between which two structures?
questions.question: The seminal vesicles are located between which two structures?

options.A: The rectum (posteriorly) and the base of the urinary bladder (anteriorly)
options.C: The urinary bladder and the pubic symphysis
options.D: The ureter and the vas deferens

explanations.A: Correct. Each seminal vesicle is a coiled tubular pouch lying obliquely above the prostate, between the base of the bladder in front and the rectum behind, related medially to the ampulla of the vas deferens; this rectovesical position is why the vesicles can be palpated on digital rectal examination in disease. This position also explains why seminal vesicle pathology (e.g. invasion by prostate cancer) can be assessed by transrectal ultrasound or MRI.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The prostate lies inferior to the seminal vesicles, not on the other side of them from the rectum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pubic symphysis lies well anterior to the bladder itself, not adjacent to the seminal vesicles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ureter passes near, but is not one of the two structures the seminal vesicle is sandwiched between; the vas deferens lies medial to the vesicle, not on an opposite side.

questions.title: The penis is embryologically homologous to which female structure?
questions.question: The penis is embryologically homologous to which female structure?

explanations.A: Correct. Both the penis and the clitoris develop from the same indifferent primordium, the genital tubercle, which elongates under androgen influence in the male to form the penis and remains relatively small in the female to form the clitoris; both retain corpora cavernosa-like erectile tissue and a glans. Recognising this shared origin also explains why both structures can develop erectile engorgement and share some innervation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The labia majora are homologous to the scrotum, both developing from the labioscrotal (genital) swellings.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The labia minora are homologous to the ventral penile shaft skin around the spongy urethra, both developing from the urogenital (urethral) folds, not to the penis as a whole.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bartholin's glands are homologous to the bulbourethral (Cowper) glands, not to the penis.

questions.title: The seminal vesicles receive their arterial supply mainly from which artery?
questions.question: The seminal vesicles receive their arterial supply mainly from which artery?

explanations.A: Correct. The seminal vesicles are supplied mainly by branches of the middle rectal artery (with a variable contribution from the inferior vesical artery), both being visceral branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery that reach the vesicles from below and behind. This dual supply is why the middle rectal artery is deliberately preserved or ligated with care during pelvic surgery near the seminal vesicles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior rectal artery, a continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery, supplies the upper rectum, not the seminal vesicles.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The internal pudendal artery supplies the perineum (external genitalia, anal canal), not the seminal vesicles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The obturator artery supplies the medial thigh and hip region via the obturator canal.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT considered a content of the spermatic cord as it traverses the inguinal canal?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT considered a content of the spermatic cord as it traverses the inguinal canal?

explanations.A: Correct. Within the inguinal canal and scrotum, testicular venous drainage exists as the multiple interconnecting channels of the pampiniform plexus; these veins condense into a single testicular vein only after the cord terminates near the deep inguinal ring, so a "single testicular vein" as such is not a content of the cord itself. This distinction matters clinically because varicocele repair targets the plexus of veins within the cord, not a single named vein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pampiniform venous plexus is the actual venous content of the spermatic cord, providing countercurrent heat exchange that keeps the testis cool.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The testicular artery is a core content of the spermatic cord, running within the cremasteric and internal spermatic fascia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vas deferens is the defining content of the spermatic cord, running along its posterior aspect.

questions.title: Which lobe of the prostate lies related to the urogenital diaphragm inferiorly and to the ejaculatory ducts superiorly as they enter the gland?
questions.question: Which lobe of the prostate lies related to the urogenital diaphragm inferiorly and to the ejaculatory ducts superiorly as they enter the gland?

explanations.A: Correct. The posterior lobe lies behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts, extending down to rest on the urogenital diaphragm; it is the lobe most accessible to digital rectal examination and the site of origin of most prostate cancers. This posterior, sub-ductal position is also why most prostate adenocarcinomas, which characteristically arise in the posterior (peripheral) zone, are detected by rectal palpation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The anterior lobe (isthmus) is a thin fibromuscular band in front of the urethra with essentially no glandular tissue and no relation to the ejaculatory ducts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The median lobe lies between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts, not below them against the urogenital diaphragm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lateral lobes flank the urethra on either side and form the main bulk of the gland, without this specific inferior/ejaculatory-duct relation.

questions.title: Spasm of which muscle can cause pain referred to the thigh muscles supplied by the sacral plexus, because the plexus lies directly on its anterior (pelvic) surface?
questions.question: Spasm of which muscle can cause pain referred to the thigh muscles supplied by the sacral plexus, because the plexus lies directly on its anterior (pelvic) surface?

explanations.A: Correct. The sacral plexus is formed on the anterior surface of piriformis, so spasm or inflammation of piriformis can irritate the plexus (including the sciatic nerve) and produce pain referred to the thigh and buttock muscles the plexus supplies — the basis of piriformis syndrome. This anatomical relationship underlies "piriformis syndrome," where sciatica-like thigh and buttock pain occurs without a true disc lesion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Obturator internus lies on the lateral pelvic wall and forms the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa; the sacral plexus does not lie directly on it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Levator ani forms the pelvic floor below the plexus, not a surface the plexus lies directly upon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Coccygeus lies posterior to the sacral plexus near the sacrospinous ligament but is not the muscle the plexus rests on.

questions.title: What structure connects (provides communication between) the vas deferens and the prostatic urethra?
questions.question: What structure connects (provides communication between) the vas deferens and the prostatic urethra?

explanations.A: Correct. The ejaculatory duct is formed by the union of the ampulla of the vas deferens with the duct of the seminal vesicle, and it runs through the substance of the prostate to open into the prostatic urethra at the seminal colliculus, providing the anatomical continuity between the vas deferens and the urethra. Recognising the ejaculatory duct as the true conduit, rather than the blind prostatic utricle beside it, avoids a common exam mix-up at the seminal colliculus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The prostatic utricle is a small blind pouch opening on the seminal colliculus, a Müllerian remnant, not a conduit connecting the vas deferens to the urethra.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ductus (duct) of the epididymis is proximal to the vas deferens, continuous with it, but does not itself connect to the urethra.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The urethral crest is a longitudinal ridge on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra on which the seminal colliculus sits; it is a landmark, not a conduit.

questions.title: The spongy (penile) urethra begins within which structure?
questions.question: The spongy (penile) urethra begins within which structure?

options.A: The bulb of the penis (proximal corpus spongiosum)

explanations.A: Correct. The spongy urethra begins as the membranous urethra pierces the perineal membrane and enters the bulb of the penis, the expanded proximal part of the corpus spongiosum; it then runs the length of the penis within the corpus spongiosum to the external urethral meatus. This is why urethral catheterisation or instrumentation must respect the corpus spongiosum's course rather than assuming the urethra runs within a corpus cavernosum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The paired corpora cavernosa are the erectile bodies dorsal to the spongiosum and do not contain the urethra.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The tunica albuginea is the fibrous capsule surrounding each erectile body, not a space that contains the urethra.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Buck's fascia is the deep fascia enclosing all three erectile bodies together; it is a covering layer, not the structure the urethra runs within.

questions.title: Regarding Müllerian-inhibiting hormone (MIH/anti-Müllerian hormone) in the male fetus, which of the following is true?
questions.question: Regarding Müllerian-inhibiting hormone (MIH/anti-Müllerian hormone) in the male fetus, which of the following is true?

options.A: It causes regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts
options.B: It stimulates development of the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts
options.C: It is secreted by the Leydig cells of the fetal testis
options.D: It stimulates development of the paramesonephric ducts

explanations.A: Correct. Müllerian-inhibiting hormone (anti-Müllerian hormone) is secreted by the Sertoli cells of the fetal testis and causes regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts in the male, so that the uterus, uterine tubes and upper vagina do not develop; simultaneously, testosterone from the Leydig cells maintains and virilises the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts. Loss-of-function mutations in MIH or its receptor cause persistent Müllerian duct syndrome, in which an otherwise normal male retains a uterus and tubes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mesonephric duct development is maintained by testosterone from the fetal Leydig cells, not by MIH.
explanations.C: Incorrect. MIH is secreted by the Sertoli cells (the supporting cells of the seminiferous tubules), not the steroidogenic Leydig cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. MIH suppresses, rather than stimulates, paramesonephric duct development — the opposite of its actual action.

questions.title: The lymphatic drainage of the ovary, the testis, and most of the uterine (fallopian) tube is to which group of lymph nodes?
questions.question: The lymphatic drainage of the ovary, the testis, and most of the uterine (fallopian) tube is to which group of lymph nodes?

explanations.A: Correct. The gonads (ovary and testis) and most of the uterine tube originate high on the posterior abdominal wall during development and descend carrying their blood and lymphatic supply with them; their lymphatics therefore follow the gonadal vessels retroperitoneally to drain into the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at the level of L1-L2, rather than into the pelvic node groups. This shared retroperitoneal drainage route is exactly why testicular or ovarian cancer staging focuses on the para-aortic nodes rather than the groin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Superficial inguinal nodes drain structures of true cutaneous/labioscrotal or lower-limb origin (e.g., vulva, scrotal skin, lower limb), not the gonads themselves.
explanations.C: Incorrect. External iliac nodes mainly drain the cervix, upper vagina and structures along the external iliac vessels, not the gonads.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Internal iliac nodes drain most pelvic viscera supplied by internal iliac branches (bladder, rectum, prostate), not the gonads, which drain along their own embryonic vessels.

questions.title: Which structure is closely related to the lateral fornix of the vagina, placing it at risk of injury during hysterectomy at this level?
questions.question: Which structure is closely related to the lateral fornix of the vagina, placing it at risk of injury during hysterectomy at this level?

explanations.A: Correct. The ureter passes close to the lateral fornix of the vagina, just below the point where the uterine artery crosses over it ("water under the bridge"); this proximity is why the ureter is vulnerable to injury or ligation during clamping of the uterine vessels at hysterectomy, and can be palpated through the lateral fornix. Recognising this relationship is why surgeons deliberately identify and mobilise the ureter before clamping the uterine vessels in a hysterectomy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ovarian artery runs in the suspensory ligament of the ovary, well above the level of the vaginal fornices.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The obturator nerve runs on the lateral pelvic wall toward the obturator canal, away from the vaginal fornices.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The internal iliac vein lies on the lateral pelvic wall, not directly adjacent to the lateral vaginal fornix.

questions.title: The labia minora develop from which embryonic structure?
questions.question: The labia minora develop from which embryonic structure?

explanations.A: Correct. In the absence of high androgen levels, the paired urethral (urogenital) folds remain unfused in the female and form the labia minora, flanking the vestibule; in the male the equivalent folds fuse over the urethral groove to form the ventral shaft skin around the spongy urethra. In males, the same urogenital folds fuse over the urethral groove instead, which is why hypospadias (failure of this fusion) leaves an abnormal urethral opening along the penile shaft.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The labioscrotal swellings remain unfused in the female to form the labia majora, not the labia minora.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The genital tubercle forms the clitoris (or penis), not the labia minora.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cloacal membrane breaks down early to establish the urogenital and anal openings; it is not the direct source of the labia minora.

questions.question: The part of the broad ligament found between the ovary and the uterine (fallopian) tube is called the?

explanations.A: Correct. The mesosalpinx is the upper free part of the broad ligament lying between the uterine tube (superiorly) and the mesovarium/ovary (inferiorly), forming a short mesentery for the tube. Keeping the three broad-ligament subdivisions straight (mesosalpinx-tube, mesovarium-ovary, mesometrium-uterus) is a frequent source of confusion on pelvic anatomy exams.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mesovarium is the fold of broad ligament that attaches the anterior border of the ovary to the posterior layer of the broad ligament, not the part between the ovary and the tube.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The mesometrium is the largest, lowermost part of the broad ligament, related to the body of the uterus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The suspensory ligament of the ovary is a separate peritoneal fold carrying the ovarian vessels from the pelvic wall to the ovary, not a subdivision of the broad ligament proper between tube and ovary.

questions.title: The seminal vesicles develop as an outgrowth of which embryonic duct?
questions.question: The seminal vesicles develop as an outgrowth of which embryonic duct?

explanations.A: Correct. Under the influence of testosterone, the distal mesonephric (Wolffian) duct gives off a lateral outgrowth just before it reaches the urogenital sinus; this outgrowth becomes the seminal vesicle, while the duct itself becomes the epididymis, vas deferens and ejaculatory duct. Testosterone acting locally (paracrine) on the adjacent mesonephric duct drives this outgrowth, which is why disorders of androgen action can leave the seminal vesicles underdeveloped.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The paramesonephric duct regresses in the male under MIH and does not contribute to the seminal vesicle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ureteric bud is a separate outgrowth of the mesonephric duct that forms the ureter, renal pelvis and collecting system, not the seminal vesicle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The urogenital sinus forms the bladder and parts of the urethra; the seminal vesicle buds from the mesonephric duct near, but proximal to, the sinus.

questions.question: The labia majora drain lymph primarily to which group of nodes?

explanations.A: Correct. The labia majora, developing from the labioscrotal swellings (homologous to the scrotum), retain a cutaneous-type lymphatic drainage to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, the same first-echelon nodes that drain the scrotal skin and perineum. This is the anatomical basis for why vulvar carcinoma is staged primarily by groin (inguinal) lymph node involvement rather than pelvic node involvement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Para-aortic nodes drain the gonads (ovary/testis), which follow a separate, retroperitoneal embryological drainage route unlike the labia majora.
explanations.C: Incorrect. External iliac nodes drain deeper pelvic structures such as the cervix and upper vagina, not the vulval skin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deep inguinal nodes receive efferents from the superficial inguinal nodes and the glans clitoris/penis, not the primary drainage site for the labia majora as a whole.

questions.title: Failure of development (aplasia) of one paramesonephric duct, with normal development of the other, results in which uterine anomaly?
questions.question: Failure of development (aplasia) of one paramesonephric duct, with normal development of the other, results in which uterine anomaly?

explanations.A: Correct. If one paramesonephric duct fails to develop while the other develops normally, only one horn and one uterine tube form, producing a unicornuate uterus, often with a single functioning ovary/tube on that side and a rudimentary or absent horn on the other. A unicornuate uterus is clinically important because it is associated with a higher risk of infertility, ectopic pregnancy and preterm labour than a normally fused uterus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Uterus didelphys results from complete failure of fusion of two otherwise normally developed paramesonephric ducts, producing two separate uteri and cervices, not from aplasia of one duct.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A bicornuate uterus results from partial failure of fusion of the two ducts (both present, incompletely joined), not from loss of one duct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A septate uterus results from failure of resorption of the midline septum after otherwise normal fusion, with both ducts present and fused externally.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT covered by peritoneum?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT covered by peritoneum?

options.D: Posterior wall of the uterine body

explanations.A: Correct. The peritoneum reflects forward off the isthmus of the uterus onto the bladder to form the uterovesical pouch, so the anterior surface of the supravaginal cervix (and the upper vagina) is left bare of peritoneum, separated from the bladder by loose connective tissue rather than a peritoneal layer. This peritoneal gap is also the surgical plane exploited when the bladder is mobilised off the cervix during a hysterectomy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior wall of the cervix, along with the posterior fornix of the vagina, is covered by peritoneum that dips down to form the recto-uterine pouch (of Douglas).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fundus of the uterus is covered by peritoneum on all its surfaces, continuous with the broad ligament laterally.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior wall of the uterine body is covered by peritoneum, forming the anterior wall of the recto-uterine pouch.

questions.title: Which part of the male urethra is its widest and most distensible part?
questions.question: Which part of the male urethra is its widest and most distensible part?

explanations.A: Correct. The prostatic urethra, running through the substance of the prostate, is the widest and most dilatable segment of the male urethra; the seminal colliculus projects into its posterior wall. This distensibility is clinically relevant because prostatic urethral strictures are less common than membranous or bulbar strictures, which occur at the narrower, more fixed segments.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The membranous urethra, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter as it crosses the deep perineal pouch, is the narrowest and least distensible part of the urethra.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The bulbar urethra within the corpus spongiosum is wider than the membranous urethra but not as wide as the prostatic urethra.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The navicular fossa is a small dilation just proximal to the external meatus, not the widest overall segment.

questions.title: The uterine (fallopian) tube develops from which embryonic structure?
questions.question: The uterine (fallopian) tube develops from which embryonic structure?

explanations.A: Correct. The unfused cranial (upper) part of each paramesonephric duct becomes a uterine tube, opening into the peritoneal cavity at its funnel-shaped fimbriated end, while the fused caudal parts of the two ducts form the uterus and upper vagina. The caudal, fused parts of the two ducts instead form the uterus and upper vagina, so a single embryonic duct system gives rise to the entire female genital tract from tube to upper vagina.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mesonephric duct regresses in the female (persisting only as vestigial remnants such as Gartner's duct) and does not form the uterine tube.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The urogenital sinus forms the bladder, urethra and lower vagina, not the uterine tube.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The genital ridge gives rise to the gonad (ovary/testis) itself, not the duct system.

questions.title: Sensory innervation of the lower third of the vagina is supplied mainly by which nerve?
questions.question: Sensory innervation of the lower third of the vagina is supplied mainly by which nerve?

explanations.A: Correct. The lower third of the vagina, derived from the urogenital sinus, is somatically innervated (touch, pain, temperature) by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4), the same nerve that supplies the perineum and external genitalia, which is why this part of the vagina is sensate. This somatic-versus-visceral split in vaginal innervation is also why procedures on the lower vagina need local anaesthesia while upper vaginal/cervical manipulation is comparatively painless without it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The upper two-thirds of the vagina, of paramesonephric origin, is supplied by the visceral (autonomic) uterovaginal plexus and is relatively insensitive to touch, unlike the pudendal-innervated lower third.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the upper medial thigh and adjacent labial skin, not the vaginal wall itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the labia majora/mons skin, not the lower vaginal mucosa.

questions.title: Anabolic androgens (e.g., nandrolone) have historically been used therapeutically for which of the following indications?
questions.question: Anabolic androgens (e.g., nandrolone) have historically been used therapeutically for which of the following indications?

explanations.A: Correct. Anabolic androgens increase bone matrix formation and muscle mass, and were historically used to help manage osteoporosis (particularly in older or debilitated patients); this use has been largely superseded by bisphosphonates, SERMs and other agents with fewer androgenic side effects, but it remains the classically taught indication. Modern practice favours bisphosphonates or SERMs for osteoporosis because they lack the virilising and cardiovascular side effects that limit long-term anabolic androgen use.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute intermittent porphyria is managed with hemin and glucose, not anabolic androgens (androgens can in fact precipitate porphyric attacks).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypercalcemia of malignancy is treated with isotonic saline, bisphosphonates or calcitonin, not androgens.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Precocious puberty is treated by suppressing, not adding, sex-steroid activity (e.g., with GnRH agonists), the opposite of giving an anabolic androgen.

questions.title: Finasteride, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor used in benign prostatic hyperplasia, acts mainly by which mechanism?
questions.question: Finasteride, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor used in benign prostatic hyperplasia, acts mainly by which mechanism?

options.A: Decreasing conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
options.B: Blocking alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in prostatic smooth muscle
options.D: Inhibiting aromatase-mediated conversion of testosterone to estrogen

explanations.A: Correct. Finasteride inhibits type II 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT) within the prostate; because DHT is the main driver of prostatic glandular growth, lowering DHT shrinks the gland over months and slowly relieves obstructive BPH symptoms. Because finasteride acts on gland volume rather than smooth-muscle tone, patients are counselled that maximal symptom benefit may take three to six months to appear.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Blocking alpha-1 receptors in prostatic smooth muscle is the mechanism of the alpha-blockers (e.g., tamsulosin), not finasteride.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Direct androgen-receptor antagonism is the mechanism of agents like flutamide or bicalutamide, not finasteride, which acts upstream at the enzyme that generates the receptor's main ligand.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Finasteride does not affect aromatase or estrogen synthesis; it is specific to 5-alpha-reductase.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT an adverse effect typically associated with parenteral (injectable) testosterone ester therapy in a boy?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an adverse effect typically associated with parenteral (injectable) testosterone ester therapy in a boy?

options.B: Premature closure of the epiphyseal growth plates

explanations.A: Correct. Hepatotoxicity (cholestatic jaundice, peliosis hepatis) is characteristically a risk of the orally active, 17-alpha-alkylated androgens (e.g., methyltestosterone), which resist first-pass hepatic metabolism; parenteral testosterone esters largely bypass this first-pass exposure and are not typically associated with significant liver toxicity. This is why hepatotoxicity monitoring is emphasised for oral androgen formulations but not routinely required for testosterone injections or transdermal preparations.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Excess androgen accelerates epiphyseal maturation and can cause premature closure of the growth plates, stunting final height in a boy — a genuine risk of parenteral testosterone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Priapism (prolonged, painful erection) is a recognized adverse effect of androgen therapy, including parenteral testosterone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral aromatization of exogenous testosterone to estradiol can cause gynecomastia, a genuine adverse effect of testosterone therapy by any route.

questions.title: Which drug affords rapid, direct symptomatic relief of lower urinary tract symptoms in BPH by relaxing prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle, and is licensed for this use?
questions.question: Which drug affords rapid, direct symptomatic relief of lower urinary tract symptoms in BPH by relaxing prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle, and is licensed for this use?

explanations.A: Correct. Tadalafil, a long-acting PDE5 inhibitor, is licensed for daily use in BPH-related lower urinary tract symptoms; by increasing cGMP it relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate, bladder neck and detrusor, giving symptomatic relief within days, faster than the months needed for the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors to shrink the gland. Because tadalafil shares the PDE5-inhibitor drug class with erectile dysfunction agents, prescribers must still screen for concurrent nitrate use before starting it for BPH.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Finasteride works by shrinking glandular volume over several months via DHT reduction, not by providing rapid smooth-muscle relaxation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dutasteride, like finasteride, is a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor with the same slow, volume-reduction mechanism, not a fast symptomatic agent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Doxazosin, an alpha-1 blocker, is also a fast-acting BPH agent, but the printed source names tadalafil specifically for this item.

questions.title: Leuprolide, a GnRH agonist analogue used in prostate cancer, produces its therapeutic effect mainly through which mechanism?
questions.question: Leuprolide, a GnRH agonist analogue used in prostate cancer, produces its therapeutic effect mainly through which mechanism?

options.A: Continuous (non-pulsatile) receptor stimulation, downregulating pituitary GnRH receptors and suppressing gonadotropin release
options.B: Direct blockade of androgen receptors in prostatic tissue
options.D: Direct inhibition of testicular steroidogenesis independent of the pituitary

explanations.A: Correct. Unlike the normal pulsatile release of endogenous GnRH, leuprolide is given continuously; this constant receptor occupancy paradoxically downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors after an initial "flare" of LH/FSH release, ultimately suppressing gonadotropin secretion and driving testosterone down to castrate levels, achieving medical (chemical) castration. This is why anti-androgen "flare cover" is co-administered for the first few weeks of GnRH agonist therapy in men with bulky metastatic prostate cancer, to blunt the initial testosterone surge.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Direct androgen-receptor blockade is the mechanism of anti-androgens such as bicalutamide, an agent often combined with, not equivalent to, a GnRH agonist.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 5-alpha-reductase inhibition is the mechanism of finasteride/dutasteride, unrelated to GnRH receptor pharmacology.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leuprolide acts centrally at the pituitary (and hypothalamic axis); it does not directly inhibit testicular Leydig-cell steroidogenesis independent of gonadotropin suppression.

questions.title: Visual disturbances (e.g., blue-tinged vision, altered colour perception) are a recognized adverse effect of PDE5 inhibitors because of cross-reactivity with which enzyme?
questions.question: Visual disturbances (e.g., blue-tinged vision, altered colour perception) are a recognized adverse effect of PDE5 inhibitors because of cross-reactivity with which enzyme?

explanations.A: Correct. PDE5 inhibitors are not perfectly selective and show some cross-reactivity with PDE6, the phosphodiesterase isoform found in retinal photoreceptors that is part of the phototransduction cascade; inhibiting PDE6 alters visual signal processing and produces the characteristic transient blue-tinged vision and light sensitivity, more prominent with sildenafil than with tadalafil. Sildenafil has a higher affinity for PDE6 than tadalafil, which is why blue-tinted vision is reported more often with sildenafil than with the other PDE5 inhibitors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. PDE3 inhibition affects cardiac contractility and vascular tone (relevant to drug interactions with nitrates via a different pathway), not the visual effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. PDE4 is mainly expressed in inflammatory and airway smooth-muscle cells; it is not implicated in the visual side effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Guanylate cyclase generates cGMP upstream of PDE5 action; it is not the enzyme responsible for the cross-reactivity that causes visual disturbance.

questions.title: Raloxifene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), is used clinically for which of the following?
questions.question: Raloxifene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), is used clinically for which of the following?

options.A: Prevention and treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis
options.C: Endometrial stimulation alongside estrogen replacement therapy
options.D: Treatment of active, metastatic breast cancer

explanations.A: Correct. Raloxifene acts as an estrogen-receptor agonist on bone (reducing resorption and increasing density, so is approved for prevention and treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis) while acting as an antagonist on breast and endometrial tissue, giving it a tissue-selective SERM profile distinct from either estrogen or tamoxifen. This tissue-selective profile is why raloxifene is sometimes described as a "designer estrogen" that captures bone benefit while avoiding breast and endometrial stimulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Raloxifene does not relieve, and can even worsen, vasomotor symptoms such as hot flashes, unlike hormone replacement therapy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Raloxifene is an estrogen-receptor antagonist in the endometrium (unlike tamoxifen), so it does not stimulate endometrial proliferation; this is part of why it avoids tamoxifen's endometrial cancer risk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Raloxifene is used to reduce the risk of invasive breast cancer in high-risk women, not to treat established active or metastatic breast cancer, for which tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors are used instead.

questions.title: Tadalafil is contraindicated in patients taking which class of drugs, because of the risk of severe, potentially life-threatening hypotension?
questions.question: Tadalafil is contraindicated in patients taking which class of drugs, because of the risk of severe, potentially life-threatening hypotension?

explanations.A: Correct. Both nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors such as tadalafil raise intracellular cGMP in vascular smooth muscle (nitrates by donating nitric oxide, tadalafil by preventing cGMP breakdown); co-administration causes an exaggerated, synergistic fall in blood pressure that can be severe and life-threatening, so concurrent use is contraindicated. Patients are specifically counselled to disclose PDE5 inhibitor use to any physician considering nitrate therapy (e.g., for chest pain), since the interaction can be fatal even with short-acting nitrates taken hours apart.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beta-blockers are not absolutely contraindicated with tadalafil, though additional blood-pressure lowering should be monitored; the mechanism-specific, dangerous interaction is with nitrates.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thiazide diuretics can contribute to hypotension in general but do not share the specific cGMP-mediated synergistic mechanism that makes the nitrate interaction dangerous.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ACE inhibitors are used cautiously with PDE5 inhibitors but are not the classic absolute contraindication taught for this drug class.

questions.learning_objective: Tadalafil and nitrates both raise vascular cGMP, so together they cause dangerous synergistic hypotension

questions.title: Which adverse effect of combined oral contraceptives (OCPs) is attributed to the estrogen component rather than the progestin?
questions.question: Which adverse effect of combined oral contraceptives (OCPs) is attributed to the estrogen component rather than the progestin?

options.A: A small increase in breast cancer risk

explanations.A: Correct. A small increase in breast (and cervical) cancer risk associated with combined OCP use is attributed mainly to the estrogenic component's proliferative effect on hormone-sensitive tissue, in contrast with several other listed adverse effects, which are more closely tied to the progestin component of older formulations. Because this risk is small and the absolute numbers are debated, clinicians weigh it against OCPs' well-established reduction in ovarian and endometrial cancer risk when counselling patients.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acne and hirsutism are androgenic side effects driven by progestins with androgenic activity (e.g., older second-generation progestins), not by the estrogen component.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Weight gain and fluid retention with older, higher-dose formulations were mainly attributed to the progestin's mineralocorticoid-like/androgenic activity, not the estrogen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mood changes and depression have classically been attributed more to the progestin component of combined OCPs.

questions.title: Which of the following is true regarding the peripheral zone of the prostate?
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the peripheral zone of the prostate?

options.B: Is the most common site of origin of BPH nodules
options.C: Is relatively resistant to both carcinoma and inflammatory processes
options.D: Is lined by a single layer of secretory cells with no basal cell layer

explanations.A: Correct. The peripheral zone, which makes up roughly 70% of prostatic glandular tissue and gives rise to the majority of prostate carcinomas, characteristically contains corpora amylacea — eosinophilic, concentrically laminated proteinaceous concretions that form within gland lumina and increase in number and size with advancing age. Their presence is a normal histologic feature of aging peripheral-zone acini rather than a marker of disease, and they are a classic teaching point distinguishing peripheral from central and transition zone tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Benign prostatic hyperplasia nodules characteristically arise in the transition zone surrounding the urethra, not the peripheral zone, which is why BPH and peripheral-zone carcinoma can coexist without one causing the other.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is the central zone, not the peripheral zone, that is relatively resistant to both carcinoma and inflammatory prostatitis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Normal prostatic glandular epithelium is composed of two cell layers — a luminal secretory columnar layer overlying a discontinuous basal cell layer — and loss of this basal layer is a key histologic clue to adenocarcinoma.

questions.title: Which of the following is true regarding Sertoli cells?
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding Sertoli cells?

options.A: Have apical cytoplasmic infoldings with an indistinct lateral cell border
options.B: Are the primary source of testosterone within the testis
options.C: Undergo continuous mitotic division throughout adult life
options.D: Have their tight junctions located outside the tubule wall, at the interstitium

explanations.A: Correct. Sertoli cells are tall, irregularly shaped supporting cells extending from the basement membrane to the lumen of the seminiferous tubule; their lateral and apical plasma membranes form complex, deeply interdigitating folds around developing germ cells, which is why their cell boundaries appear indistinct on routine light microscopy. This irregular, folded architecture lets a single Sertoli cell physically support and nurture many germ cells at different stages of spermatogenesis simultaneously.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Testosterone is produced by Leydig (interstitial) cells lying between seminiferous tubules, not by Sertoli cells, although Sertoli cells concentrate testosterone via androgen-binding protein to support spermatogenesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sertoli cells are terminally differentiated after puberty and essentially do not divide in the adult testis; it is the spermatogonia at the base of the epithelium that continue to divide.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The tight junctions that form the blood-testis barrier lie between adjacent Sertoli cells near the base of the seminiferous epithelium, not at the outer boundary between the tubule and the interstitium.

questions.learning_objective: Sertoli cells show apical infoldings and an indistinct border on light microscopy, distinct from Leydig cell and germ cell features.

questions.title: The vas deferens is characterized by which of the following features?
questions.question: The vas deferens is characterized by which of the following features?

options.A: It has a thick, three-layered muscularis
options.B: It has the widest lumen of any part of the male excretory duct system
options.C: It lacks a muscularis and relies on ciliary transport of sperm
options.D: Its epithelium and wall are histologically identical to the epididymis

explanations.A: Correct. The vas deferens is characterized by an unusually thick three-layered smooth muscle coat — inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal — surrounding a narrow, irregular lumen. This thick musculosa is the single most useful histologic feature for identifying the vas deferens and provides the strong peristaltic contractions that propel sperm during ejaculation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vas deferens lumen is narrow and irregular in outline; it is the epididymis, particularly its proximal portion, that has a wider, more regular lumen.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vas deferens is a highly muscular duct whose thick wall generates the peristaltic contractions responsible for expelling sperm at emission, not a passive ciliary conduit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While the vas deferens shares a pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia similar to the epididymis, what distinguishes it is precisely its markedly thicker three-layered muscular wall, which the epididymal duct lacks.

questions.learning_objective: The vas deferens is identified histologically by its thick three-layered muscularis around a narrow lumen.

questions.title: Sertoli cells help maintain a supply of high levels of local testosterone by which of the following?
questions.question: Sertoli cells help maintain a supply of high levels of local testosterone by which of the following?

options.A: Synthesizing testosterone de novo from cholesterol
options.C: Converting testosterone to dihydrotestosterone via 5-alpha reductase
options.D: Secreting inhibin, which directly raises testosterone levels

explanations.A: Incorrect. Testosterone is synthesized de novo from cholesterol by Leydig cells, not Sertoli cells; Sertoli cells instead concentrate testosterone that Leydig cells have already produced.
explanations.B: Correct. Sertoli cells secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP) into the seminiferous tubule lumen; ABP binds testosterone and keeps it at a high local concentration within the tubular fluid, which is necessary to sustain the later stages of spermatogenesis. ABP secretion is stimulated by FSH acting on Sertoli cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone by 5-alpha reductase occurs mainly in peripheral androgen target tissues such as the prostate and skin, and is not the mechanism by which Sertoli cells raise intratubular testosterone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inhibin acts on the anterior pituitary to suppress FSH secretion; it does not directly raise testosterone levels.

questions.learning_objective: Sertoli cells concentrate testosterone locally via androgen-binding protein rather than synthesizing it.

questions.title: Which of the following is true regarding the CatSper protein?
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the CatSper protein?

options.A: It is present in the plasma membrane of the sperm tail
options.B: It is located in the acrosome and mediates the acrosome reaction
options.C: It is a mitochondrial protein of the middle piece involved in ATP synthesis
options.D: It is a nuclear protein that compacts sperm chromatin

explanations.A: Correct. CatSper is a sperm-specific calcium channel located in the plasma membrane of the principal piece of the tail. Calcium influx through CatSper drives the whip-like, high-amplitude flagellar beating known as hyperactivated motility, which sperm need to penetrate the cumulus oophorus and zona pellucida.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The acrosome reaction is mediated by a distinct set of membrane receptors and exocytotic machinery in the sperm head, not by CatSper, which is confined to the tail.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ATP synthesis in the middle piece is carried out by the mitochondrial sheath, a structurally and functionally distinct component from the CatSper channel.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sperm chromatin compaction is achieved by protamines replacing histones in the nucleus, an unrelated process to the CatSper tail-membrane channel.

questions.title: What is the lining of the intralobular and smaller interlobular ducts of the resting breast?
questions.question: What is the lining of the intralobular and smaller interlobular ducts of the resting breast?

options.A: Two layers of cuboidal cells with an underlying myoepithelial layer
options.B: A single layer of tall columnar secretory cells without myoepithelial cells
options.C: Stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the nipple skin

explanations.A: Correct. In the resting breast, the intralobular and smaller interlobular ducts are lined by two layers of cuboidal epithelial cells with an underlying, discontinuous layer of myoepithelial cells. This contract to aid fluid movement and provide a supportive basal layer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A single layer of tall secretory columnar cells describes the alveolar epithelium of the actively lactating breast, not the resting ducts, and it too retains an outer myoepithelial layer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stratified squamous epithelium is found only at the nipple surface and the most proximal segment of the lactiferous duct near its orifice, not throughout the intralobular and interlobular ducts.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Simple squamous epithelium is not a normal lining of the breast ductal system at any level.

questions.title: Which of the following is a characteristic histologic feature of the fallopian tube, particularly its ampulla?
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic histologic feature of the fallopian tube, particularly its ampulla?

options.A: Its mucosa is thrown into complex primary, secondary, and tertiary folds
options.B: It has a smooth, unfolded mucosa lined by simple squamous epithelium
options.C: It has a thick keratinized stratified squamous lining similar to the vagina
options.D: It has glandular endometrial-type mucosa with spiral arteries

explanations.A: Correct. The fallopian tube mucosa is elaborately folded into primary, secondary, and even tertiary plicae, an arrangement most complex in the ampulla. The folds are lined by simple columnar epithelium containing both ciliated cells, which help transport the oocyte, and secretory (peg) cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tubal mucosa is highly folded, not smooth, and is lined by simple columnar epithelium, not simple squamous epithelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A thick keratinized stratified squamous lining is characteristic of the vagina and ectocervix, not the fallopian tube.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glandular mucosa with spiral arteries describes the uterine endometrium, a structurally distinct organ from the fallopian tube.

questions.title: Arrest and failure of chromosome separation during the first meiotic division of a primary oocyte most typically results in which of the following?
questions.question: Arrest and failure of chromosome separation during the first meiotic division of a primary oocyte most typically results in which of the following?

options.D: A balanced reciprocal translocation carrier state

explanations.A: Incorrect. Turner syndrome (45,X) most often arises from loss of a sex chromosome, frequently of paternal origin or through a post-zygotic mitotic error, rather than being the classic teaching consequence of maternal meiosis I nondisjunction.
explanations.B: Correct. Human primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division from before birth until ovulation, sometimes for decades. This prolonged arrest is thought to predispose to nondisjunction — failure of homologous chromosome pairs to separate correctly — which is the classic mechanism producing trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), with risk rising sharply with advancing maternal age.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) can also arise from meiotic nondisjunction, it is trisomy 21 that is the standard teaching example most closely linked to maternal meiosis I errors and advanced maternal age.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A balanced translocation is a structural chromosomal rearrangement transmitted from a carrier parent, an entirely different mechanism from numerical nondisjunction during meiosis.

questions.title: Which of the following induces penile erection?
questions.question: Which of the following induces penile erection?

options.A: Increased cGMP and nitric oxide (NO) release from cavernosal nerve endings and endothelium
options.B: Increased sympathetic norepinephrine release causing cavernosal artery vasoconstriction
options.C: Increased circulating angiotensin II acting on cavernosal smooth muscle
options.D: Increased calcium influx into cavernosal smooth muscle

explanations.A: Correct. Parasympathetic stimulation releases nitric oxide from cavernosal nerve endings and vascular endothelium, which activates guanylate cyclase in cavernosal smooth muscle to raise intracellular cyclic GMP; cGMP lowers intracellular calcium and relaxes the smooth muscle of the corpora cavernosa and their arterioles, allowing blood inflow and veno-occlusive trapping that produces erection. This is also the target of phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, which prolong cGMP action by blocking its breakdown.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sympathetic activity, via norepinephrine on alpha-adrenergic receptors, maintains cavernosal smooth muscle contraction and penile flaccidity; withdrawal of sympathetic tone, not an increase, permits erection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that would oppose, not produce, the smooth muscle relaxation required for erection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Erection depends on a fall, not a rise, in cavernosal smooth muscle intracellular calcium; increased calcium influx would instead promote contraction and detumescence.

questions.learning_objective: NO-mediated cGMP elevation relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle to produce erection.

questions.title: Which of the following statements about the scrotum is true?
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the scrotum is true?

options.A: It keeps testicular temperature cooler than core body temperature, favoring spermatogenesis
options.B: It has no independent thermoregulatory mechanism and simply follows ambient temperature
options.C: Scrotal temperature is normally 2-3°C higher than core body temperature
options.D: The pampiniform plexus warms incoming testicular arterial blood before it reaches the testis

explanations.A: Correct. The scrotum actively maintains testicular temperature roughly 2-3°C below core body temperature, through the contractile dartos and cremaster muscles that adjust testicular position relative to the body and the pampiniform venous plexus, which cools incoming arterial blood by countercurrent exchange. This cooler environment is required for normal spermatogenesis, which is impaired at core body temperature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The scrotum has active thermoregulatory mechanisms — the dartos and cremaster muscles and the pampiniform plexus — rather than passively following ambient temperature alone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Scrotal/testicular temperature is normally lower, not higher, than core body temperature; a temperature elevation, as in cryptorchidism, impairs spermatogenesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pampiniform plexus cools incoming testicular arterial blood by countercurrent heat exchange with the cooler venous blood leaving the testis, rather than warming it.

questions.learning_objective: The scrotum actively cools the testis below core temperature to support spermatogenesis.

questions.title: Which of the following represents a function of the prostate?
questions.question: Which of the following represents a function of the prostate?

options.A: Secretes a thin, milky, alkaline fluid
options.B: Produces the bulk of seminal fructose that nourishes sperm
options.C: Secretes an acidic fluid that activates sperm motility
options.D: Is the primary site of spermatozoa storage before ejaculation

explanations.A: Correct. The prostate secretes a thin, milky, alkaline fluid containing prostatic acid phosphatase, citrate, zinc, and prostate-specific antigen (PSA). This alkaline fluid helps neutralize the acidic vaginal and residual urethral environment and, through PSA-mediated proteolysis, contributes to liquefaction of the coagulated ejaculate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The bulk of seminal fructose, the main energy substrate for ejaculated sperm, is produced by the seminal vesicles, not the prostate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prostatic fluid is alkaline, not acidic, and sperm motility activation classically occurs after mixing of seminal vesicle and prostatic secretions in the ejaculate, not within the prostate alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Spermatozoa are stored mainly in the epididymis (and to some extent the ampulla of the vas deferens) before ejaculation, not in the prostate.

questions.title: A 28-year-old man who looks like a 10-year-old, has little facial hair, and is diagnosed with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Which of the following describes this condition?
questions.question: A 28-year-old man who looks like a 10-year-old, has little facial hair, and is diagnosed with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Which of the following describes this condition?

options.B: Premature closure of epiphyseal growth plates with short stature
options.C: Excessive facial and body hair growth
options.D: Early puberty with accelerated bone age

explanations.A: Correct. Without adequate testosterone during puberty, the larynx and vocal cords fail to undergo the normal androgen-driven growth and thickening, so the voice remains high-pitched into adulthood. This is one of several eunuchoid features, alongside sparse facial hair and immature genital development, seen in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Absent sex steroids actually delay, not accelerate, epiphyseal growth plate closure, producing relatively long limbs and eunuchoid body proportions rather than short stature.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Low androgen levels reduce, rather than increase, facial and body hair growth, consistent with the sparse facial hair already described in this patient.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism causes delayed or absent puberty with low, not accelerated, bone age, the opposite of what is described.

questions.title: Which of the following hormones is dominant during the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle?
questions.question: Which of the following hormones is dominant during the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle?

explanations.A: Correct. Rising estrogen secreted by the developing ovarian follicle dominates the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle, driving mitotic proliferation of the endometrial glands and stroma to rebuild the functional layer shed at the previous menstruation. This estrogen-driven regrowth restores the endometrium after the previous cycle's shedding and sets up the tissue that progesterone will later transform in the secretory phase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Progesterone becomes dominant only after ovulation, during the secretory (luteal) phase, once the corpus luteum begins secreting it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prolactin is not the driving hormone of the normal menstrual cycle; sustained hyperprolactinemia actually suppresses the cycle by inhibiting GnRH pulsatility.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Testosterone is not a normal driver of the uterine cycle in women, although small amounts are produced by the ovary and adrenal gland.

questions.title: Fertilization of the oocyte can occur up to how long after ovulation?
questions.question: Fertilization of the oocyte can occur up to how long after ovulation?

explanations.A: Correct. The ovulated secondary oocyte remains viable and capable of being fertilized for approximately 24 hours after ovulation. Beyond this window it degenerates and loses fertilizability, which is why the fertile window depends more on sperm surviving in the tract before ovulation than on the oocyte surviving after it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 72 hours considerably overstates the oocyte's fertilizable lifespan, which is closer to 24 hours.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 6 hours understates the oocyte's viability window, which extends to roughly a full day.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Five days approximates how long sperm, not the oocyte, can survive and remain capable of fertilizing within the female reproductive tract.

questions.title: Which of the following is true regarding the regulation of the follicular phase?
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the regulation of the follicular phase?

options.A: FSH stimulates proliferation of granulosa cells
options.B: LH is the principal stimulus for granulosa cell proliferation in the early follicular phase
options.C: Inhibin stimulates FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary
options.D: Estrogen from the dominant follicle exerts only positive feedback on FSH throughout the follicular phase

explanations.A: Correct. FSH from the anterior pituitary is the principal stimulus for granulosa cell proliferation within developing ovarian follicles during the follicular phase, and it also induces granulosa cell aromatase activity. This converts theca-derived androgens into estrogen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. LH acts mainly on theca cells to stimulate androgen precursor production in the early follicular phase; it is FSH, not LH, that principally drives granulosa cell proliferation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inhibin, secreted by granulosa cells, suppresses rather than stimulates FSH secretion, forming a negative feedback loop.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Estrogen exerts negative feedback on FSH for most of the follicular phase; only when estrogen reaches a sustained high level near mid-cycle does it switch to positive feedback, triggering the LH surge.

questions.learning_objective: FSH drives granulosa cell proliferation and aromatase activity during the follicular phase.

questions.question: Which of the following may be present in a 60-year-old woman as a consequence of the menopausal transition?

options.B: Increased vaginal lubrication and epithelial thickness

explanations.A: Correct. Estrogen normally favors a more protective lipid profile. Its loss after menopause is associated with a rise in serum total and LDL cholesterol, contributing to the increase in cardiovascular disease risk seen in postmenopausal women.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Estrogen loss after menopause causes vaginal atrophy, with thinning of the epithelium and reduced lubrication, not increased lubrication and thickness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Estrogen loss accelerates bone resorption, causing decreased, not increased, bone density (osteoporosis) after menopause.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Menopause is defined by the permanent cessation of menstrual cycles (amenorrhea), not by continued regular cycles.

questions.title: Which fetal cell type secretes Müllerian-inhibiting hormone (anti-Müllerian hormone), driving regression of the Müllerian ducts in the male fetus?
questions.question: Which fetal cell type secretes Müllerian-inhibiting hormone (anti-Müllerian hormone), driving regression of the Müllerian ducts in the male fetus?

explanations.A: Correct. Fetal Sertoli cells secrete Müllerian-inhibiting hormone (anti-Müllerian hormone). This acts on the ipsilateral paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct to cause its regression, preventing development of the uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper vagina in the male fetus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leydig cells secrete testosterone, which maintains and virilizes the Wolffian ducts and external genitalia; they do not secrete Müllerian-inhibiting hormone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Theca cells are a component of the postnatal ovarian follicle in the female, not a fetal testicular cell type, and are not the source of MIH.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Germ cells (spermatogonia) give rise to sperm and are not endocrine cells; they do not secrete Müllerian-inhibiting hormone.

questions.title: Which of the following is an action of progesterone on the female reproductive tract?
questions.question: Which of the following is an action of progesterone on the female reproductive tract?

options.A: Formation of thick, sticky cervical mucus hostile to sperm
options.B: Production of thin, watery, elastic cervical mucus that facilitates sperm penetration
options.C: Proliferation of the endometrial glands and stroma
options.D: Increased cervical os dilation to facilitate sperm entry

explanations.A: Correct. Progesterone. This dominates after ovulation, causes the cervix to secrete thick, scanty, sticky mucus that forms a barrier hostile to sperm penetration, contrasting with the thin, elastic mucus estrogen produces around ovulation to facilitate sperm transport.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thin, watery, elastic ("spinnbarkeit") mucus that facilitates sperm penetration is produced under estrogen dominance around ovulation, the opposite of progesterone's effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Proliferation of endometrial glands and stroma is driven by estrogen in the proliferative phase; progesterone instead promotes secretory transformation and glandular differentiation, not further proliferation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Progesterone tends to keep the cervix firm and closed, not to increase dilation for sperm entry, which instead is favored around ovulation under estrogen.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.learning_objective: Progesterone thickens cervical mucus, opposing estrogen's thin, sperm-friendly periovulatory mucus.

questions.title: What causes bleeding at the onset of menstruation?
questions.question: What causes bleeding at the onset of menstruation?

options.A: Rapid withdrawal of progesterone as the corpus luteum regresses
options.B: A sudden surge of luteinizing hormone (LH) at midcycle
options.C: A rise in progesterone maintaining the endometrium
options.D: Rupture of the dominant ovarian follicle

explanations.A: Correct. In the absence of pregnancy the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase, causing progesterone and estrogen levels to fall rapidly. This hormone withdrawal triggers spiral artery vasoconstriction and ischemic shedding of the endometrial functional layer, producing menstrual bleeding.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The LH surge occurs at mid-cycle and triggers ovulation, an event roughly two weeks before menstruation, not the bleeding itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A rise in progesterone maintains and stabilizes the secretory endometrium; it is a fall, not a rise, in progesterone that precipitates shedding.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Follicular rupture at ovulation is an ovarian event that precedes menstruation by about two weeks and does not itself cause endometrial shedding.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.learning_objective: Menstruation is triggered by progesterone (and estrogen) withdrawal at corpus luteum regression.

questions.title: What happens in the endometrium during the secretory phase under progesterone influence?
questions.question: What happens in the endometrium during the secretory phase under progesterone influence?

options.A: A decidual reaction occurs, with glandular glycogen storage
options.B: The endometrial glands proliferate rapidly under mitotic stimulation
options.C: The functional layer of the endometrium sloughs off and is shed
options.D: Spiral arteries first form and become newly vascularized for the first time

explanations.A: Correct. Progesterone acting on the estrogen-primed endometrium during the secretory phase induces glandular glycogen accumulation and stromal decidual change, transforming the endometrium into a nutrient-rich, secretory tissue prepared to support a possible implanting blastocyst. This secretory transformation, unlike the earlier proliferative phase, is not primarily about further glandular growth but about functional differentiation in readiness for pregnancy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rapid mitotic proliferation of the glands is the hallmark of the earlier, estrogen-driven proliferative phase, not the secretory phase, in which glandular growth slows and secretory activity dominates instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Shedding of the functional layer is the event of menstruation, which follows the secretory phase after progesterone withdrawal, not an event of the secretory phase itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Spiral arteries are already present from earlier in the cycle and elongate and coil further during the secretory phase; they do not first form at this stage.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.learning_objective: The secretory phase, under progesterone, produces decidual change and glandular glycogen storage.

questions.title: Which of the following induces the onset of puberty?
questions.question: Which of the following induces the onset of puberty?

options.A: Pulsatile release of GnRH from the hypothalamus
options.B: Continuous, non-pulsatile high-dose GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus
options.C: A sudden fall in circulating leptin levels
options.D: Loss of adrenal cortex sensitivity to ACTH

explanations.A: Correct. Puberty is triggered when the hypothalamus resumes pulsatile GnRH release. This reactivates pituitary gonadotroph responsiveness and drives the pubertal rise in LH, FSH, and downstream gonadal sex steroid secretion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Continuous, non-pulsatile GnRH exposure actually desensitizes and downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors, suppressing rather than stimulating gonadotropin secretion — the principle exploited by GnRH agonist therapy to treat precocious puberty.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rising, not falling, leptin levels are thought to be permissive for pubertal onset, signaling adequate energy reserves to the hypothalamus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The adrenal cortex-ACTH axis is a separate endocrine system from the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis that governs puberty.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.learning_objective: Pulsatile, not continuous, GnRH release triggers pubertal reactivation of the gonadal axis.
